# Rails fetch: concurrent transfers without pods queueing for a node's NICs

Status: built (`internal/agent/rails_fetch.go`, `rails_serve.go`, `rails_jobs.go`, `checkpoint_spread.go`).
Scope: those files and the agent chart's `rails.*` values.

## 1. The problem

In a scale-out of a 2-node GB300 instance (2 engine ranks of about 840 GB each, 4 companions of 12 to 154 MB,
all fetched over the rails), the rails moved each engine rank's data in 59 s (838 GB at 13.25 GiB/s), yet the
group restore started 3 min 15 s after the pods were created. Companions moved their data in 0.3 s and took 11
to 57 s end to end. The transfers waited for each other, not for the rails. No record of this run is under
`results/`.

## 2. Why the transfers wait

1. A rails pod holds every RDMA NIC of its node through one DRA claim (`ClaimTemplate`), so a second rails pod
   on the node cannot schedule until the first ends.
2. Before this design, every transfer created its own pods: a serve pod on each source node and a fetch pod on
   its own node. Concurrent fetches from one source queued for its NICs.
3. Small checkpoints paid the full pod cost (10 s or more of scheduling, sandbox and readiness) for well under
   a second of data, while holding NICs a large transfer needed.
4. Source choice ignored what a node was doing: picking a node that was itself waiting to fetch blocked that
   node's own fetch.

## 3. Design

### 3.1 Small checkpoints: the peer tier, on clusters with no L2

With the rails tier on and a catalog configured, a checkpoint smaller than `rails.minSize` goes to the HTTP peer
tier and never starts a rails pod: the rails fetch finds a source, returns `errRailsSmall`, and `EnsureLocal` tries
the peers first. With rails off, `rails.minSize` does not route anything and the usual tier order applies. That tier
needs no pod, NIC claim or shared storage: the fetching agent reads the files from the agents that hold them,
authenticated, from several sources at once (`fetchFromPeer`). The size is known from the peer listing. Large
checkpoints keep the rails, and the peer tier stays the fall-back for both. The default comes from
measurement (section 4, step 1).

With no L2, a checkpoint lives only on its capture node and on nodes that restored it since, and a group
restore needs every member's. Losing the one node that holds a companion would lose the whole group's capture.
So once a group capture is recorded, every member smaller than `rails.minSize` is copied to the capture nodes
of the group's other members, through their agents' `ensure-local` endpoint (`checkpoint_spread.go`
`spreadSmallCheckpoints`). Best effort: the copies run after the capture is recorded, reach only the other capture
nodes (not nodes that restore a rank later), and a member of unknown size is not copied. A failed copy is logged and
retried by the next restore's own fetch; it never fails the capture.

### 3.2 One rails pod per node, shared by every transfer

- Each node has one rails pod, named `nvsnap-rails-serve-<node label value>`. It runs
  `bedrock-peer serve --root <checkpoint dir> --max-fetchers N` in the background, and each of the node's own
  fetches beside it, handed over through files in the checkpoint directory (`rails_jobs.go`). bedrock-peer
  processes share a node's NICs (a fetch only opens outgoing connections), so a node can send and receive at
  once, which a node that is the only source of one checkpoint while fetching another needs. There are no
  fetch pods.
- A fetch names its checkpoint with `--prefix <checkpoint id>`. The checkpoint directory is mounted writable,
  and the pod gets the larger of the serve and fetch budgets.
- A fetcher that needs a source creates its rails pod; `AlreadyExists` means it is there and is used. A pod
  that is already terminating is never reused; the fetcher waits for it to go, then creates a new one. A rails
  pod the scheduler cannot place is given up after 15 s.
- Lifetime: before using a pod, a fetcher patches `nvsnap.io/rails-wanted-until` on it to the end of its
  fetch's budget. The node's agent deletes the pod once that time has passed and no fetch from another node
  still lists it as a source. The delete carries the pod's resourceVersion as a precondition, so a patch that
  lands after the agent read the pod cancels the delete.
- The pod is owned by its node's agent pod, and the agent's start-up sweep (`sweepRailsPods`) removes it.

### 3.3 Sources that are not busy fetching

`fetchOverRails` ranks the nodes that list the checkpoint:

1. Nodes not fetching for themselves come first. An agent marks its rails pod `nvsnap.io/rails-fetching: "true"`
   while the pod runs any fetch of the node (`railsFetchStarted`); `railsNodeStates` reads the mark. A fetch pod
   of an older agent, labelled `nvsnap.io/rails-for`, still counts.
2. Among those, a node whose rails pod is already Ready comes first.
3. A node that is fetching is used only when no other node holds the checkpoint; then transfers still queue.

### 3.4 What stays as it is

- The NIC claim, the security context, the copy into the checkpoint directory under the fetch marker, the
  free-space check, and the fall-through to the next tier on any failure.
- A cancelled fetch is stopped before the directory is used again (`stopRailsJob`): one not yet started is
  withdrawn; a running one is asked to stop and waited for, and one that does not stop within a minute ends
  with its pod. Until that is confirmed, `EnsureLocal` tries no other tier into the directory.

## 4. Measurements behind the defaults

Neither run below has a record under `results/`; GB300 nodes, nvsnap build not recorded.

### Step 0: bedrock-peer behaviour

bedrock-peer 0.1.0 (fd09ff3), one serve pod, two fetch pods on other nodes:

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| `--prefix` layout | Files land at the top of `--dest`, beside bedrock-peer's own `.bedrock-peer-*` entries, which the agent removes. Mode, mtime and owner are kept. |
| New checkpoints | The listing is per request: a directory created under `--root` after `serve` started was fetched. |
| Concurrency | Two 32 GiB fetches overlapped (`active=2`, at most 4), each about 3 s, same content digest. The files were in the source's page cache, so the rate is an upper bound. |
| Memory | 9.05 GB idle, 9.29 GB peak with two fetchers: about 9 GB fixed plus about 115 MB per fetcher. The 32 Gi limit covers `--max-fetchers 4` (`rails.serve.memory`, with `rails.serveMaxFetchers`). |

### Step 1: the HTTP peer tier

An agent read real checkpoints' files from another node's agent through `/manifest` and `/file`,
authenticated, 8 files at a time as `fetchFromPeer` does, to `/dev/null`:

| Data | Files | Time | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12 MB (a NATS checkpoint) | 58 | 0.06 s | 0.20 GB/s |
| 153 MB (a frontend checkpoint) | 62 | 0.15 s | 1.0 GB/s |
| 1.1 GB (part of an engine rank's checkpoint) | 451 | 0.59 s | 1.9 GB/s |
| 4.3 GB | 515 | 1.0 s | 4.3 GB/s |
| 17.2 GB | 743 | 3.0 s | 5.8 GB/s |

A rails fetch takes at least 10 s before its first byte, then moves about 14 GB/s, so the two break even near
100 GB. Reads to `/dev/null`, possibly from the source's page cache, make the peer rates an upper bound, so
the default is set well below break-even: `rails.minSize` = 16 GiB (`railsDefaultMinBytes`), about 3 s over
the peer tier. Not yet confirmed with writes to disk end to end.

## 5. Tests

Unit tests use the fake clientset (`rails_fetch_test.go`, `rails_serve_test.go`, `rails_jobs_test.go`,
`checkpoint_spread_test.go`) and cover: a checkpoint below `rails.minSize` skips the rails and is fetched from
peers with L2 absent; after a group capture, small members are copied to the other members' capture nodes
only, a failed copy does not fail the capture, and members at or above `rails.minSize` are not copied; the shared
pod is created once, reused on `AlreadyExists`, not reused while terminating, and patched before a fetch is
handed to it; the reaper deletes only after `wanted-until` with no fetch listing the node, and a precondition
conflict leaves the pod; source ranking; `--prefix` in the job's arguments and a cancelled job stopped before
the wait returns; the pod never Ready, the job never started, or bedrock-peer exiting non-zero each fall
through to the next tier, while a cancelled fetch that may still run does not; the start-up sweep.

## 6. Not addressed here

- Sandbox failures right after a rails pod ends (the CNI cannot find a NIC the previous pod released) are in
  the cluster's networking. Fewer rails pods make them rarer, not gone.
- The rest of a restore (CRIU, GPU memory load, remap, resume) is outside this design.
